auxiliary_passages.statement_original: We denote the topological dual space of a separable Banach space, $V$, by $V'$. For complex separable Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H,\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2$, we let $\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2$ denote the Hilbert tensor product space, and we denote the $r$th Schatten class by $S_r(\mathcal H)$, which is the class of bounded linear operators $A:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ with bounded $r$th Schatten norm, i.e, $\|A\|_{S_r}<\infty$, $1\leq r\leq\infty$. We denote the respective subspaces of self-adjoint and non-negative definite operators by $(\cdot)^\dagger$ and $(\cdot)^+$, respectively. We remark that the cone of non-negative definite elements satisfies $S_r(\mathcal H)^+\subseteq S_r(\mathcal H)^\dagger$, and that $S_\infty(\mathcal H)\cong(S_1(\mathcal H))'$. We furthermore denote the tensor product operator $h\otimes g:\mathcal H_1\to\mathcal H_2$, which is the bounded linear operator $(h\otimes g)v=\langle v,g\rangle h$, $v,g\in\mathcal H_1,h\in\mathcal H_2$. We emphasize that the meaning of $\cdot\otimes\cdot$ will be clear from the context.

evidence.location: Notation — operator spaces and rank-one convention

auxiliary_passages.resolution: The actual main theorems use S1 trace topology, not S2 Hilbert-Schmidt topology. The source uses S_infinity for the bounded-operator dual of S1; no compact-only convention at infinity is imposed. The inner product is linear in its first variable under the rank-one formula.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Throughout this paper, we use the notation $I=[0,1]$ for the unit interval in order to refer to a process indexed by a parameter $\eta\in I$, while we use the parameter $u\in[0,1]$ to refer to re-scaled time. The set of all continuous functions $f:I\to V$ is denoted by $C_V=C(I,V)$.
auxiliary_passages.resolution: Eta is the sequential fraction, u is rescaled time, and omega is frequency. T is sample size, N is local block length, M is the number of time-grid points, and x in Theorem 3.1 is the transformation exponent. These are distinct parameters.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: For a measurable space $(T,\Sigma)$ with $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, we define $L_V^p(T,\mu)$ as the Banach space of all strongly measurable functions $f:T\to V$ with finite norm $\|f\|_{L_V^p(T,\mu)}=(\int\|f(\tau)\|_V^p d\mu(\tau))^{1/p}$, $1\leq p<\infty$. If $T\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\mu$ is the Lebesgue measure on $T$, we simply write $L_V^p(T)$. Given a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal A,P)$, we write $L_V^p=L_V^p(\Omega,\mathcal A,P)$ for the space of all strongly measurable functions $X:(\Omega,\mathcal A,P)\to(V,\mathcal B_V)$ with $\|X\|_{V,p}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_V^p)^{1/p}<\infty$. The (conditional) expectation of $X\in L_V^p$ thus exist (in the sense of a Bochner integral), and the $k$th moments $k\leq p$ can be naturally defined using tensor products. We use $\overset{\mathscr D}{\Longrightarrow}$ for process convergence, $\overset{\mathscr D}{\longrightarrow}$ for distributional convergence of a vector, and $\overset{\mathbb P}{\longrightarrow}$ for convergence in probability. Finally, we let $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ denote the floor function and for two positive sequences, $(a_T)$, $(b_T)$, we write $a_T\sim b_T$ if $\lim_{T\to\infty}a_T/b_T=1$.
auxiliary_passages.resolution: Strong moments use Bochner integration; the theorem branches use high p even though earlier assumptions initially say p>0. Process convergence is in the continuous-path space with the indicated Banach norm. Standard asymptotic O, o and their probability variants retain their usual meaning.

\sup_\omega\sup_{u\in U_M}\sup_{\eta\in I}\left\|\eta\big(\widehat{\mathscr F}_{u,\omega}(\eta)-\mathscr F_{u,\omega}\big)\right\|_{S_1}=o_P(1),\qquad(T\to\infty).\tag{3.30}
\]
To prove (3.30), we make use of the mixing condition exhibiting polynomial decay, where the speed of the decay is controlled by the parameter $\rho$ in condition (3.28). auxiliary_passages.statement_original: In case of compact operators on infinite-dimensional spaces, an open neighborhood $D\subset\mathbb C$ containing the spectrum, say $\sigma(A)$, of a compact operator $A$ will also contain the origin. auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
More specifically, it follows from the latter work that, for fixed $u$, the functional Cramer representation of the approximating stationary process $\{X_t^{(u)}\mid t\in\mathbb Z;u\in[0,1]\}$ is given by
\[
X_t^{(u)}=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{i\omega t}dZ_{u,\omega}\quad a.e.\text{ in }\mathcal H,\tag{2.4}
\]
where $\{Z_{u,\omega}:\omega\in(-\pi,\pi]\}$ is an $\mathcal H$-valued right-continuous orthogonal increment process for each $u\in[0,1]$.
auxiliary_passages.resolution: Z in the component and coherence definitions is the Cramer orthogonal-increment process. This binds the symbol without importing an external theorem. D28 preserves the later equality between the spectral density and moments of Z, rather than replacing it by a density of increment covariances.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: To this end, consider the case where the Hilbert space arises as the direct sum of Hilbert spaces, i.e., $\mathcal H=\mathcal H_1\oplus\mathcal H_2$. Then, we may write $\{X_{t,T}\mid t=1,\ldots,T,T\in\mathbb N\}=\{(X_{t,T,1},X_{t,T,2})^\top\mid t=1,\ldots,T,T\in\mathbb N\}$, where we refer to $\{X_{t,T,j}\mid t=1,\ldots,T,T\in\mathbb N\}$ as the $j$th component process, which takes values in the Hilbert space $\mathcal H_j$ $(j=1,2)$.
auxiliary_passages.resolution: This is the direct-sum model for coherence, not the tensor-product model used for separability. Component Z processes are the components of A9 for the stationary approximants.

auxiliary_passages.statement_original: We conclude this section with the important observation that the assumptions $\Delta>0$ and $r>0$ are crucial for the statement in Theorem 4.2. unresolved_source_conventions.note: The source calls E(X_h tensor X_0) a covariance without subtracting means. A main-text search for zero, mean and centering, together with inspection of the definitions and assumptions, found no process mean-zero restriction. No missing centering hypothesis is inserted.
The replacement field uses the absolute index k before a supremum over t; the stationary reduction later anchors X_k with replacement at zero. This indexing difference is retained.

Earlier p>0 wording differs from the p>=1 Bochner convention. Actual S1 results retain Assumption 3.2 II and high moment requirements; the S2 relaxation in the remark is not applied. The identity branch prints p>=6, while a proof-technical p/2 integer comment is not promoted to an extra theorem hypothesis.

The printed estimator divides by floor(eta N), has a single interpolation factor on the final self-product, is zero for floor zero, and has an unclosed parenthesis. Its claimed path continuity and positivity do not follow from these formulas and window conditions without further qualifications. No conventional replacement estimator or positive-definite window restriction is substituted.

The display uses k_f, whereas the following line defines kappa_f. The two kappa regimes share their boundary and both stated bounds are retained there. N=T^alpha is printed without integer rounding; the growth exponent alpha differs from the later significance level.

Upsilon starts as an operator on continuous S_r paths, but its time derivatives are given in L(S1) and the displayed map is evaluated pointwise. The original typing is retained without inventing a stronger operator field.

The source switches L1 to L in the D_r formula. Square roots are not holomorphic at zero; the finite-rank recommendation alone does not specify subspace identification, treatment of zero extension, or the eta=0 endpoint. Appendix E is not read.

Point evaluations at U_M are specified on an L1 space, which normally consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. A representative or sufficient time regularity must be supplied; the source formula is preserved.

Gamma and Sigma are defined only by (B.11) and (B.12). Those formulas and joint covariance details remain unresolved because appendix bodies are excluded. Corollary 3.1 uses tau without squares where Theorem 3.1 uses tau squared.

The main-text consistency condition is saved as A4. The exact choice of p as a function of rho and kappa is deferred to Theorem C.3 and remains unresolved; the heuristic p=7 is not a universal replacement.
Formal composition and explicit expansions disagree about extra h and eta inside phi. A7 preserves both expansions, including unclosed outer parentheses; D16/D20 preserve the formal definitions.
The author uses the word linear for a specified scaling identity, with a path-valued right-hand side lacking an explicit eta evaluation. Additivity is not substituted.

The second factors are conjugated, while the quadratic form uses ordinary transpose despite permitting proper complex Brownian motions. V_k and U have squared-entry notation, not matrix squares. Limiting nonsingularity does not supply a finite-sample inverse convention. The extra closing parenthesis in (3.37) is retained.
The theorem writes a positive diagonal function on all I using positive-entry matrix notation, whereas (3.34) allows nonnegative g and the examples vanish at eta=0. The source difference is retained.

The dotted sequence counts multiplicities; the undotted sequence lists distinct values. The ratio of eigenvalue sums equals the trace version only with the appropriate multiplicity interpretation. The specialized theorems retain their simple-spectrum conditions.

The complex Hilbert-space rearrangement is printed without conjugate-space qualifications. The separability ratio also prints integration limits with differentials in the opposite order from the later theorem. Neither is silently rewritten.

The source equates a spectral density with moments of cumulative Z, maximizes a complex inner product without an explicit real-part or modulus convention, and identifies cross-spectrum singular-vector maximizers with marginal leading eigenfunctions. Those identifications require additional justification and are preserved as source assertions. The ratio is not replaced by a different standard canonical-correlation definition.

Theorems 3.3-3.5 allow sigma=0; Theorem 3.6 omits a separate sigma qualifier. Following claims about pivotal statistics still require the positive-definite limit and nonsingularity conditions of Theorem 3.2. The Gaussian-limit statements do not acquire those additional assumptions.
The marginal eigenvalue chain contains a comma before its last eigenvalue rather than another greater-than sign. The statement is retained exactly.
The first argument of population r_d lacks eta, although the next display defines an eta-dependent mean square root. Both are retained without substituting a normalized stationarity measure.
T_d denotes a deviation r_d in Section 2.4 and an accuracy s_d in Section 4.2. This source-local change is recorded; the two are related by s_d=1-r_d in the nested-model setup.

Equation (4.4) prints f_d(eta) B_d eta) - g_dd(1) B_d(1), with a missing opening argument parenthesis and a different f/g placement from (4.1). The original formula is retained rather than repaired to the expected pivotal expression.

Equation (2.18) uses strict > with Latin v and a following prose subscript/superscript typo. The later equality case s_d*=nu conflicts with that definition. The hypotheses (4.9) and (2.17), however, are equivalent under the strict definition and monotonicity; there is no separate error in that equivalence.

The first-exceedance estimator uses lower q_alpha, while the accuracy rejection rule uses upper q_(1-alpha,d0). The limiting variables may depend on d and need not be independent. No finite search cutoff, empty-minimum convention or quantile continuity restriction is specified.
Consistency is asserted for any alpha_T tending to zero, without a rate restriction. This is recorded as the source claim, without adding uniform-tail assumptions or certifying its proof.
